Text:
A group of health care providers caring for a patient can be one of three types:

{{c1::dependent}}

{{c1::independent}}

{{c1::interdependent}}
Back Extra:
Cue: the deciding question is who directs the work — the leader alone (dependent), each member over his or her own area (independent), or everyone together (interdependent).

Pitfall: only the interdependent arrangement is a true team — dependent and independent providers are working as a group, not a team.

Text: In a {{c1::dependent::group type}} group, each member is {{c2::told what to do — and often how to do it}} by the group leader.
Back Extra:
Why: relying on the leader for task assignments, troubleshooting, and virtually all decisions limits the group's ability to adapt and deliver critical care in an uncontrolled field environment.

Distinguish: independent-group members may also get support and guidance from a leader, but they act on their own areas without waiting for an assignment.

Text: In an {{c1::independent::group type}} group, each member is responsible for {{c2::his or her own area}}.
Back Extra:
Meaning: the member's own area can be a physical space or a set of tasks.

Distinguish: unlike dependent-group members, independent members act without waiting for an assignment — but unlike a true team, each pursues an individual goal (start the IV, splint the arm) rather than a unified one.

Pitfall: the classic failure of independent-group work is the perfectly splinted and packaged trauma patient who arrives at the ED dead from an unrecognized, poorly managed airway.

Text: EMTs and other health care providers who work {{c1::interdependently::group type}} are functioning as a {{c2::true team}}.
Back Extra:
Why: each provider may still be assigned a particular area or task, but all providers work together with shared responsibilities, accountability, and a common goal.

Distinguish: independent-group members may also work on the same patient — the difference is that each of them pursues an individual goal instead of a shared one.

Text: One of the five essential elements of effective team performance is a shared goal: every provider, from EMT to paramedic to emergency physician, must be committed to a common goal — typically, {{c1::the best possible patient outcome}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: the alarming phrases that reveal a missing shared goal — "Why take the time to splint the patient if the ED will only undo it?" and "No point doing good CPR if the paramedic isn't even trying to save the patient."

Distinguish: the shared goal says where the team is headed; clear roles and responsibilities (another of the five elements) say who does what to get there.

Text: One of the five essential elements of effective team performance, {{c2::clear roles and responsibilities}}, means that to achieve a common goal, each provider must know {{c1::what needs to be done}} and {{c1::what is expected of him or her}}.
Back Extra:
Ex: pit crew CPR — every intervention needed during a cardiac arrest (compressions, defibrillation, airway management, vascular access, medications) is defined in advance, and providers are trained for each role.

Distinguish: a shared goal sets the destination; clear roles and responsibilities make sure each provider knows his or her own part in reaching it.

Text: The {{c1::team leader}} is the team member who provides role assignments, coordination, oversight, centralized decision making, and support so the team can accomplish its goals.
Back Extra:
Cue: the team leader is often defined by policy, procedure, or statute — and may be the most senior provider or the one with the highest level of certification.

Distinguish: a team leader does more than assign and decide — he or she also helps members do their jobs, working together with them and facilitating coordination.

Text: A team leader who simply commands others is not leading a team — he or she is merely directing a {{c1::dependent group::group type}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the key differentiation between a team leader and a group leader — a team leader helps individual members do their jobs, not only providing support but working together with them and facilitating coordination.

Why: relying on one commander for virtually all decisions limits a group's ability to adapt and deliver critical care in an uncontrolled field environment.
